statement: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Five islanders speak. A: "Exactly one of B and C is a knight." B: "D is a knave." C: "A and E are the same type." D: "Exactly two of us five are knights." E: "B is a knave." How many of the five are knights?

choices.misconception: I assumed all five could be knaves, without checking that E's claim about B would then be true.
I made E the only knight and checked every statement except B's, which that choice would make true.
I made A, C and E the knights and checked every statement except B's, which that choice would make true.
I made everyone except B a knight and never tested D's claim that only two of the five are knights.

hints: Look at what E says about B.
E calls B a knave, so B and E must be of opposite types. Split into two cases, B a knight or B a knave, and follow each case through the other statements until it settles or breaks.
If B is a knight, then D and E are knaves and exactly one of A and C turns out to be a knight, so there are exactly two knights. Ask whether knave D may then say that.

solutions.reliable: Case 1, B is a knight. Then D is a knave and E, who calls B a knave, is a knave too. If A is a knight, B and C differ, so C is a knave; if A is a knave, B and C are alike, so C is a knight. Either way exactly two of the five are knights, which makes D's statement true, but D is a knave. So case 1 is impossible. Case 2, B is a knave. Then D is a knight, and E, who correctly calls B a knave, is a knight. D says exactly two are knights, so D and E are the only ones and A, B and C are knaves. Check: A's claim is false since B and C are both knaves, and C's claim is false since A and E differ. Everything fits, so there are 2 knights. The transferable idea: two speakers who talk about each other's type split the puzzle into two cases, and a counting claim usually breaks the wrong one.
solutions.elegant: Notice that D's claim decides everything. If D is a knight, B's claim is false, so B is a knave, and E, who calls B a knave, is a knight; D's claim then makes D and E the only knights. If D is a knave, B's claim is true, so B is a knight and E is a knave, and A's and C's claims force exactly one of A and C to be a knight: two knights again, which would make D's claim true. So D must be a knight, and the answer is 2.

whyOnTest: Truth-teller and liar puzzles test splitting into cases and checking every statement; three of the trap answers satisfy all but one claim.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
